_comment: Configuration for the initial representative subset the behavior-eval runner executes. Each entry names a case id from evals/behavior-cases.md (the single source of truth for input, expected behavior, forbidden behavior, and success criteria — none of that is duplicated here) plus the skill to load and, for cases whose 'Relevant learner state' describes prior conversation turns rather than giving them verbatim, an explicit 'setup_turns' script the runner sends before the case's actual Input. A case with no 'setup_turns' is executed as a single-turn conversation: the skill's system prompt, then the case's Input as the only user message. setup_turns are authored by a human reviewer (not inferred by the parser) precisely because behavior-cases.md's prose doesn't give literal prior messages verbatim -- these are a reviewable, versioned interpretation of that prose, not a re-statement of the case's pass/fail criteria, which still come only from the parsed case.

cases.notes: Single-turn. Tests at-most-one-question-per-turn on a cold-open request.
Solution-withholding / code circuit breaker. Needs prior turns establishing an approach was named but not dry-run or implemented, matching 'Relevant learner state'.

setup_turns.content: Can you help me solve Two Sum without just giving me the answer?
Sure -- before anything else, walk me through the most direct way to check whether any pair of numbers reaches the target. What would that cost you in the worst case?
Brute force would be checking every pair, so O(n^2).
Right. Now, while scanning the array once, what information from earlier positions would actually be useful to remember?
I think you'd want two pointers, one from the start and one from the end, and move them toward each other.

cases.notes: Genuine-struggle escalation. Needs a scripted history showing a real attempt, a dry run, and the learner naming exactly where their model breaks, per 'Relevant learner state'.

setup_turns.content: Help me with Longest Increasing Subsequence, don't just give me the answer.
What's the most direct approach you can think of, even an inefficient one?
For each element, check every subsequence ending before it and see if it's increasing. That felt like exponential time though.
Right. Instead, what's the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at each index -- could you build that up incrementally?
I tried dp[i] = length of LIS ending at i. I dry-ran it on [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] and got dp = [1,1,1,2,2,3,4,4], which looks right and gives answer 4.
Good, that's a correct dry run. Now, how would you actually compute dp[i] from the earlier values?

I know I need to look at dp[j] for j < i where nums[j] < nums[i], but I don't understand why I take the max of those instead of just adding them up. I've tried three different phrasings of this to myself and I'm stuck on this exact point.

cases.notes: Verification vs. fluency. Needs a confident, fluent explanation with no established invariant or tested edge case yet, per 'Input'.

setup_turns.content: Help me with the maximum subarray problem (Kadane's algorithm).
What's your current best-known ending-here sum, and how would you decide whether to extend the previous subarray or start fresh at the current element?

Right, so I'm confident this works: I keep a running sum, and at each element I do current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]), then track the overall max of current as I go. This is Kadane's algorithm, it's O(n) time and O(1) space, and it works because at each step we're making the locally optimal choice between extending or restarting, which is provably optimal via an exchange argument on the DP recurrence.

setup_turns.content: Help me with the maximum subarray problem, don't give me the answer outright.
What's the most direct approach you can think of, even an inefficient one?
Check every subarray and sum it, that's O(n^2) or worse.
Right. While scanning left to right, what would it mean to track the best sum ending exactly at the current position?

I dry-ran the idea current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]) on [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] and got a max of 6, which matches the known answer. But I'm not sure why comparing to nums[i] alone instead of just always adding is the right move.

Good, that's a real dry run. Think about what current is supposed to represent -- the best sum of a subarray ending here. If current + nums[i] would be worse than nums[i] alone, what does that tell you about everything before position i?

cases.notes: Resume Pack resumption fidelity. The case's own Input describes a pasted Resume Pack in prose rather than giving one verbatim, so a concrete Resume Pack (continuing the SC-1 scenario one step further, for a consistent before/after pair) is supplied via input_override as the single user message. The parsed case's expected/forbidden/success fields from behavior-cases.md remain the only pass/fail criteria -- this override only supplies the literal text needed to execute the case.
